run.question:
1. List the tables in the database and tell me the verification code from the holmes_eval_223 table
2. I'm experiencing slow queries with this SQL: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345
   Analyze why this query is slow and suggest how to fix it

report.summary: Database investigation (SQL target m0-otel-20260909, database testdb, read at 2026-11-23T18:40:39Z–18:41:28Z). (1) The database contains exactly two tables in schema dbo: holmes_eval_223 and orders. holmes_eval_223 holds one row (id=1, category=eval_test, created_at 2026-11-23T18:40:22.777) whose verification_code is HOLMES-MSSQL-EVAL-223-j2w7p9. (2) For the slow-query question the structural cause is clear and observed: dbo.orders has only one index, the clustered primary key on id, with no index on customer_id, so the predicate customer_id = 12345 can only be satisfied by a Clustered Index Scan (plan: PhysicalOp="Clustered Index Scan", EstimatedRowsRead=10000, TableCardinality=10000, no Index Seek node), and the optimizer emitted a MissingIndexGroup hint with Impact=93.9833 for equality on [customer_id]. However, the 'slow' premise was NOT reproduced on this instance at query time: orders holds only 10,000 rows in 64 pages (~0.5 MB), and the cached plan for the parameterized form (@1 smallint)SELECT * FROM [orders] WHERE [customer_id]=@1 shows 1 execution at 667 microseconds with 64 logical reads; index usage stats show 0 seeks and 6 scans on the PK. Additionally, the literal 12345 matches zero rows because customer_id values only span 1–1000, so this exact query is both cheap and empty here. So: the access path is explained and a covering nonclustered index on customer_id is the correct fix for growth, but there is no observed evidence of actual slowness, and Query Store (READ_WRITE, 0 MB of data) holds runtime history only for the INSERT that seeded the table, not for this SELECT. Histories outside this database, client-side latency and lock/blocking contention were not observable.

claims.text: The database has exactly two tables, both in schema dbo: holmes_eval_223 (type table) and orders (type table).

dbo.holmes_eval_223 has columns id (int, PK), category (nvarchar), verification_code (nvarchar), created_at (datetime, default getdate()) and its only index is the primary key PK__holmes_e__3213E83F690ED3FD on id.
holmes_eval_223 contains one row: id=1, category='eval_test', created_at=2026-11-23T18:40:22.777, verification_code='HOLMES-MSSQL-EVAL-223-j2w7p9'.

dbo.orders has columns id (int, PK), customer_id (int), order_date (date), total_amount (decimal), status (nvarchar) and its sole index is the clustered primary key PK__orders__3213E83F95F7DA4E on id (not disabled, no filter); no index has customer_id as a key or included column.

dbo.orders holds 10,000 rows (64 used pages, ~0.5 MB) with 1,000 distinct customer_id values, customer_id ranging 1–1000, and order_date ranging 2025-11-24 to 2026-11-23; the most frequent customer_id is 743 with 21 rows.
The predicate customer_id = 12345 matches zero rows: COUNT(*) for customer_id = 12345 returned 0, and customer_id only ranges 1–1000 in this table.

The cached execution plan for the parameterized form of the query, (@1 smallint)SELECT * FROM [orders] WHERE [customer_id]=@1, shows the root operator PhysicalOp="Clustered Index Scan" with EstimatedRowsRead=10000 and TableCardinality=10000, contains no 'Index Seek' text, and that one recorded execution took 667 microseconds with 64 logical reads.

The plan for a query with the same customer_id = 12345 predicate carries a MissingIndexGroup with Impact="93.9833" proposing an EQUALITY index on [dbo].[orders].[customer_id], and its statistics usage lists auto-created statistics _WA_Sys_00000002_38996AB5 on orders with SamplingPercent=100 last updated 2026-11-23T18:40:42.81.

Index usage counters for the orders clustered PK (since instance start) show user_seeks=0, user_scans=6, user_lookups=0, user_updates=10000, confirming reads on orders are served by scans and no seek supporting access exists.

Query Store is READ_WRITE with current_storage_size_mb=0 and stale_query_threshold_days=30, and its only captured query text touching orders is the seeding statement INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, order_date, total_amount, status) VALUES (...) with query_id=1, 9971 executions and max average duration 0.0274 ms; no runtime history exists for the SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 query.
No triggers, views, procedures or functions depend on dbo.orders; the only dependent object returned is the PRIMARY_KEY_CONSTRAINT PK__orders__3213E83F95F7DA4E.

The reason this query's access path is expensive by design is the absence of any nonclustered index on dbo.orders.customer_id: with only the clustered PK on id, every execution must read the whole table (10,000 estimated rows / 64 pages), a cost that grows linearly with order volume, which is the mechanism that would make it slow on a larger orders table.

The reported slowness may not originate in this database at all: on the observed data the query costs 64 logical reads and 667 microseconds, and the literal 12345 matches no row (customer_id 1–1000), so client-side latency, a non-existent-customer lookup misread as a slow query, or a different/larger environment remain unresolved alternatives.

Counter-evidence against current measured slowness: the plan cache's single execution of the SELECT * predicate recorded total_elapsed_time 667 microseconds and total_logical_reads 64, the table occupies only 64 pages (~0.5 MB) with 10,000 rows, and comparable full scans in cache completed in 1.4–2.9 milliseconds, so this database's current workload shows no slow execution of this query.

Rejected as the cause on the evidence seen: a schema trigger or dependent view/procedure multiplying work for this query — a search of sys.objects returned no trigger, view, procedure or function tied to dbo.orders, only its primary key constraint.

Add a nonclustered index on dbo.orders(customer_id); to make the current SELECT * shape covering, INCLUDE the remaining columns (order_date, total_amount, status), or preferably stop using SELECT * and read only needed columns so a narrower index on customer_id suffices. Validate the new plan shows an Index Seek instead of the Clustered Index Scan before/after deployment.

Confirm the parameter value: customer_id is an int column holding 1–1000 only, so verify whether 12345 is a valid customer identifier for the calling application; an out-of-range value returns an empty result rather than a performance problem.

Because Query Store is READ_WRITE but stores no runtime stats for this SELECT, keep it enabled and re-check its runtime stats after the query runs under real load, and capture client-side timings, to distinguish real slowness from a symptom reported without measurement.

gaps: No observed evidence that SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 is actually slow: Query Store holds runtime history only for the INSERT seed statement (query_id 1) and 0 MB of stored data, and the only plan-cache entry for the SELECT is the single execution made during this investigation (667 microseconds, 64 logical reads).

Missing-index DMV query (sys.dm_db_missing_index_details filtered to orders) returned no rows at 2026-11-23T18:40:48Z; that empty result is not evidence of absence, while the plan XML of the aggregate variant did contain a MissingIndexGroup with Impact 93.9833 on customer_id.

Whether this database is the one where users experienced slowness is unverified; the instance hosts only testdb with two tables (holmes_eval_223 and orders) totalling 10,000 order rows, so a larger production dataset, historical growth or a different environment could not be compared.

Locking/blocking contention at the time of the reported slowness could not be assessed: sys.dm_exec_requests values for blocking_session_id were redacted, and the snapshot at 2026-11-23T18:41:06Z contained only background and sleeping sessions with no active user query.

Client-side/application latency and the calling service tier of this SQL were not observable through the available SQL, Prometheus, Jaeger or Kubernetes sources; change history integration is not configured in this Run.
No latency baseline before the reported slowness exists, so no trend or regression can be inferred for this query.

Review the application code that issues this statement to confirm the customer_id value's origin (12345 is outside the seeded 1–1000 range) and replace SELECT * with an explicit column list.
Check with the application owner for end-to-end timings and error/retry logs of the caller, since the database-side execution measured here is sub-millisecond.
